en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching on the Elimination of Fear and Calamity, translated by the Qifu Qin śramaṇa Shi Shengjian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha, together with the fourfold assembly.
The assembly of disciples gathered together, and he preached the sublime and wondrous Dharma.

At that time, a virulent pestilence broke out in the kingdom of Vaiśālī; its fierce and blazing power was like a raging fire, causing countless deaths, leaving the victims with no refuge and no means of medical relief.
The king, ministers, elders, householders, and brahmins gathered for a grand deliberation:
"The kingdom has been struck by calamity; it is not merely being crushed by misfortune, but scorched by the fires of pestilence, with countless lives lost."
"By what principle and by what expedient means should we eliminate this calamity?
The Brahmins deliberated and said,
"We should establish sacrificial altars at all the city gates."
Some proposed, saying:

"We should establish a great sacrificial altar at the crossroads within the city to ward off the baleful influences. Others proposed, saying: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the narrative as found in the source text.*

"One should perform a sacrificial offering using one hundred varieties of white animals—white horses, white camels, white oxen, white sheep, white chickens, and white dogs—to suppress, pacify, and dispel [the calamity]."

At that time, within the assembly, there was an elder named Tan-ni (in the Jin language, Cai-ming), who had received the five precepts from the Buddha, practiced the ten wholesome deeds, and served as a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) who had clearly realized the stages of the Path. He then spoke these words:
"Please listen to what I have to say. Our country has met with calamities, and countless people have perished.
If, as you gentlemen propose, one harms living beings in order to save lives, how can this possibly be right?"
Because of the unwholesome deeds committed in previous lives, you now encounter this calamity.
You ought to employ skillful means to use the wholesome to ward off the evil, so as to part forever from suffering;
why instead act perversely by inflicting harm in pursuit of peace, only to endure suffering through the long night with no prospect of escape?
Then the great assembly asked Caiming,
"What proposal should be made? Caiming replied:

"In this world there is a great protector, the teacher of gods and humans throughout the trichiliocosm, who provides universal shelter and compassionately pities all sentient beings; he is named Buddha, walking alone and unchallenged through the three realms."
"If he can be enticed to descend and grace our kingdom with his presence, disasters may be eliminated.
Upon hearing this, the great assembly all concurred with the proposal; there was none who did not praise it as excellent.
Caiming also said: “The Buddha cultivated the six perfections over incalculable kalpas.

He gave away boundless kingdoms, cities, wealth, and treasures; elephants, horses, and carriages; his own head, eyes, marrow, and brain; as well as his body and wife and children. Through the precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, he disciplined himself in every lifetime beyond measure, seeking the Way of the Buddha not for his own sake, but solely for the sake of sentient beings—to rescue them from peril and distress, and to eliminate the myriad afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.”

Now that he has attained the Way of the Buddha, he accords with his original vow to travel everywhere to rescue and deliver beings, bestowing the medicine of ambrosia to eliminate the afflictions of bitter poison in this life and future lives, so that all may forever attain peace.
The assembly all said,
“What you have said is most sincere and truly refreshing. However,
since the Buddha is in Rājagṛha and King Ajātaśatru has a feud with our country, how could he possibly permit the Buddha to come here?”
Or again, some said:
"Perhaps we should allow the Buddha to come.
At that time, Caiming said:
“The Buddha has arisen in the world to rescue sentient beings from suffering; like space, he is without obstruction—whom could anyone restrain?
Like the light of the sun, all things sprout and grow, none of which fail to receive his nurturing.”
The Buddha, pitying the calamity of the kingdom, will surely come; of this there is no doubt.
You should merely dispatch high-ranking envoys with rare and precious gifts, and approach Ajātaśatru with warm words and elegant expressions of gratitude.
Furthermore, you should separately seek refuge in the Buddha, surrendering your lives with earnest and poignant sincerity.

Although his heart harbored resentment, he placed trust in the envoy’s noble character and presented him with exquisite treasures; his words were gentle and his reasoning refined, so that no matter how dire the situation, all was brought to peace.

Since ancient times, when neighboring states have been in discord and have turned upon one another in invasion and rebellion, it has always been through wise envoys—carrying famous jewels as weighty gifts and employing soft, submissive speech—that harmony and reconciliation have been achieved.
They spoke to one another in turn, wondering who could be entrusted with this mission.
At that time, the great assembly, the king, the ministers, the elders, and the householders all agreed, saying:
"Only the lay devotee, the elder Caiming, is a disciple of the Buddha; he may serve as the messenger to go and invite the Buddha."
"Why is this? Previously, the assembly initiated the proposal to invite the Buddha.
He then addressed Cai-ming:
"Only you, O Benevolent One, may go to the kingdom of Rājagṛha to exchange greetings with the king and request that the Buddha come.
At that time, Caiming accepted the mission and prepared to depart.

At that time, the great assembly all rose from their seats and withdrew to sit toward the direction of the Buddha; with palms joined and kneeling for a long time, they prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs to pay homage to the Buddha. Kneeling, they addressed Caiming:

"The Buddha is the God among Gods, whose compassion, kindness, and joy protect all living beings. We pray only that you take pity on our humble land, which has encountered a great calamity—disease and death like a fierce wild fire consuming grasses and trees—as we are all beset by distress and hardship."

Fortunately, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is like one seeking dawn in the darkness, like one longing for the morning sun in the cold, like one seeking shade and drink in the heat of summer, like one with an illness pursuing a skilled physician, or like a lost traveler seeking a guide.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will deign to descend and grant us relief, bestowing the Dharma of Ambrosia so that we may find rest and recovery.

Thereupon, Caiming accepted the command as an envoy and traveled to Rājagṛha; traversing the road directly, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and went to the gate to request an audience to present his letter, instructions, and gifts.
At that time, when King Jian heard this, Cai Ming addressed him, saying:

"We have come as envoys to your kingdom; although we were previously at odds, there has been no other grave cause for estrangement. Therefore, we first offer our devotion to remove former discord and together bring peace to the myriad people."
The Buddha has appeared in the world, his great compassion universally covering all. Our kingdom is beset by a grave affliction;

therefore, we entreat Your Majesty to request the Buddha to turn his light toward us and deign to visit our humble land to rescue us from this calamity, so that we may hope to receive his divine protection.
The King reflected silently:
"I intended to detain the Buddha so that he would not leave the country, but there is no rational way to achieve this; it is beyond my power to restrain him.

The Buddha, through his great compassion, has universally granted his presence to all ten directions; he regards both the hateful and the beloved with equanimity, making the salvation of beings his primary task. For these reasons, he cannot be detained."
He then addressed Cai-ming, saying,
"You may go to the Buddha’s dwelling and proclaim the command of your noble kingdom.
Thereupon, Cai-ming took his leave and proceeded to the Bamboo Grove, arriving at the vihāra.

Beholding the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they all paid reverent homage with their five limbs prostrate on the ground, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The kings, ministers, elders, and householders of the kingdom of Vaiśālī pay distant homage at the feet of the Buddha."
"O God among Gods, you universally compassionately care for all sentient beings, and there are none who do not receive your salvation.
Our humble kingdom has encountered calamity; we only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow your grace by sending down your light, have pity on our suffering and distress, and grant us relief."
At that time, the Buddha remained silent, granting his consent to the request.
Upon seeing that the Buddha had accepted the invitation and permitted him to go, Cai Ming was filled with immeasurable joy.

Then, the deities, devas, nāgas, and spirits within the borders of the kingdom of Rājagṛha, knowing that the Buddha had accepted the invitation and would be departing for another country, were all agitated and deeply distressed. They manifested their spiritual response and spoke to the king of that land, Ajātaśatru, saying:
“Great King, how can you remain so tranquil and free from sorrow?

Before long, you shall be separated from the Buddha, like an infant who has lost both parents; like one traveling a vast road who is deprived of water and grain; or like one in bitter cold who has lost their clothing.”
"Now that the Buddha is about to depart, the kingdom will lose its protector; such is the analogy.
Upon hearing these words spoken by the descending deities, the King’s heart was immediately moved with sorrow, and he was filled with profound grief. He reflected in silence:

"Sentient beings are obstinate and ignorant, their dispositions dull and turbid. Now that they have parted from the World-Honored One, where else can they find the whetstone of wisdom to grind and polish their dull minds?"
Who shall rescue us from the heavy transgressions of our worldly toil and the grave retributions of past lives?
Who shall instruct us to eliminate the heavy sins of all sentient beings so that they may be lightened?

We have long remained in the prison of birth and death, confined by heavy bolts; who shall again take the key of the True Dharma to open the heavy, firmly locked gates of this prison of birth and death?
We are all scorched by the dust of toil and the intense heat of the midday sun; from where can we obtain the moon-essence great pearl of the Buddha’s cool teaching to dispel this burning heat?

The king immediately ordered his carriage to be prepared and went out to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit in his usual place.
At that time, the Buddha preached the True Dharma for the king’s edification; it was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, purifying body, speech, and mind, and was pure, subtle, and wondrous.
The king’s heart was filled with joy; he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:

“Recently, the messenger from Vaiśālī invited the World-Honored One, and having learned that you have already granted permission to go there, my heart is deeply distressed, for I have no means to detain your reverence.”
"Please deign to show compassion and accept my humble request to remain in the palace for three months.
The Buddha said to the king:
"Sentient beings are pitiable; if I were to stay for three months, when would I ever be able to bring relief to those suffering from myriad afflictions?"
For countless kalpas, I have disciplined my body in suffering to seek the Way; for the sake of sentient beings, I vowed to attain Buddhahood in order to bestow the medicine of ambrosia upon them.

Now that my vow has been fulfilled—just as a person who has compounded a divine elixir and desires to save all ailments might encounter a sick person and yet, failing to keep his original oath, refuse to give it to him, he would not be a skilled physician.
If one sees a person drifting along the riverbank and does not go to rescue them, it is unbecoming of a worthy gentleman.
If one sees someone who has lost their way in the wilderness and does not show them the correct path, this is a lack of benevolence.

Out of great compassion and universal pity for all sentient beings, I travel through various kingdoms, counties, towns, and villages to rescue them from manifold sufferings and bestow the medicine of ambrosia. To those without support, I am their support; to those without refuge, I am their refuge.
The king addressed the Buddha again with earnest entreaty:
"I only beseech you to grant me your compassionate favor and permit [me] to receive [the teachings] for two months.
The Buddha still did not grant his permission.
The king, with profound earnestness, knelt for a long time with palms joined and, shedding tears, spoke, saying:
"Life is difficult to preserve; it is like a lamp lit in the open air that suddenly extinguishes when encountering the wind of impermanence."
"Now that I part from the Buddha, when shall I ever behold your venerable countenance again?
I beseech you to accept two months [of my service].
The Buddha declined once more.
The king then threw himself at the Buddha’s feet, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will extend his great compassion to me and my assembly of disciples, and grant us permission to stay for one month.
The World-Honored One, unable to bear [the king’s distress], immediately granted his request.
The king then rose and, his heart filled with joy and reverence, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid his respects, and returned to the palace.

He commanded the kitchen to prepare a meal of a hundred flavors, ensuring it was of the utmost excellence—fresh, sweet, fragrant, and pure. Within the palace, silken banners, canopies, various jewels, couches, tables, carpets, and seating arrangements were set out; the grounds were swept and repaired, and the floor was sprinkled with scented water. When all these preparations were complete, he sent word again.
When the time arrived the following day, the King stood upon the main road and, facing the World-Honored One from afar, burned incense and knelt for a long time, saying:
“O Buddha, God among Gods!
You, the Sage who perceives the proper time, I pray that you and your assembly of holy ones will turn back your divine radiance and descend to our palace to partake of a vegetarian meal.”
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded his disciples to don their dharma robes and take up their alms bowls, proceeding to the king’s invitation.

The Buddha and the assembly of noble ones arrived at the royal palace; the king, with the utmost devotion, welcomed the Buddha at the palace gate with flowers, incense, music, and dance. Once they had entered, each took his seat.
The King personally served water to the entire assembly of noble ones; with his own hands, he distributed the hundred-flavored foods, which were fresh, pure, fragrant, and sweet, all of them equally.
Day by day, he provided offerings of food, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

He commanded the outer palace to repair and fill the roads, plant trees along the streets in seven rows extending even to the riverbanks, and set up pavilions, curtains, and seating arrangements at intervals, adorned with banners and canopies so that they resembled the celestial avenues;
furthermore, he newly fashioned five hundred canopies made of the seven precious gems.
When the kingdom of Vaiśālī heard that the Buddha was about to arrive, they likewise leveled and smoothed seven rows of pathways, planted rows of trees, and prepared canopies and seats.
The king, ministers, elders, and householders each led their respective assemblies out of the city to welcome the Buddha.

When the month had come to an end, the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones emerged from the palace and reached the road; the King followed the great multitude and scattered flowers over the Buddha, which completely covered the ground.
The great assembly gathered like the autumn waters of the Ganges flowing into the vast ocean.
A white moon-jewel adorned a parasol made of the seven precious gems; the king, with hands joined in reverence, held it up and offered it to cover the World-Honored One.
The Buddha and the great assembly proceeded along the road until they reached the bank of a river.

At that time, the King presented five hundred canopies made of the seven precious gems to the Buddha; the Dragon King of the Great Ocean likewise respectfully offered five hundred canopies of the seven precious gems; the various dragons of the Ganges River also together presented five hundred canopies of the seven precious gems to the Buddha;
and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, leading the assembly of devas, further offered five hundred canopies of the seven precious gems to the Buddha.

At that time, the great multitude of Vaiśālī who came to welcome [the Buddha] were arrayed in magnificent attire: those with blue horses, blue chariots, blue parasols, and blue banners were all dressed in blue;
those with red horses and red chariots were all dressed in red;
those with yellow horses and yellow chariots were all dressed in yellow.
There were white horses and white chariots, with all their trappings white;
black horses and black chariots, with all their trappings black;
distinguished by their various colors, they were escorted by countless attendants.
The Buddha saw him from afar and told his disciples:
"If you wish to know the majestic deportment of the Heavenly Lord when he goes out on an excursion, it is like this.
The people of the kingdom of Vaiśālī welcomed the Buddha with five hundred seven-jeweled parasols; each holding their own parasol, they approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“Buddha, God among Gods!
You cover the entire world; we pray that you accept this gift of canopies.
The Buddha accepted their offering, leaving behind only one canopy.
At that time, the great assembly each harbored doubts in their hearts, wondering whether this was not the retribution for the accumulation of virtue and the performance of good deeds in past lives.

The Sea Dragon King, the Ganges Dragon King, Śakra Devānām Indra, the King of Vaiśālī, and the King of Rājagṛha each presented him with a wondrous parasol made of the seven treasures; as they all assembled together at once, they further wondered why he would not accept even one of these parasols.
Thereupon, Ānanda, perceiving that the assembly harbored doubts, knelt down with palms joined and stepped forward to address the Buddha:
"O Heaven among Heavens!
The great multitude is universally in doubt; by what cause does this occur today?"
"These two thousand five hundred and seven precious canopies have arrived simultaneously; they are offered to the World-Honored One.
Is this the retribution for roots of goodness from past lives, or is it present merit?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will resolve all our doubts.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen with single-minded concentration; I shall now resolve and eliminate the doubts you and the others hold."

In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a wheel-turning sage king named Māndhātṛ—translated in the Jin language as "Great Heaven" (Mahādeva)—who ruled over the four quarters of the world.
The king had a thousand sons, escorted by the seven treasures.
When the youngest son of the king saw his father’s royal parasol adorned with the seven treasures, he returned and asked his mother,
"When shall I be able to wear this parasol to adorn myself?"
The mother said, "O my son!
Among the king’s thousand sons, you are the youngest and smallest. If the Great King were no more, the Crown Prince would succeed him; [how much more so, then, should you]."
"If the Crown Prince passes away, the succession will pass down in order through a thousand sons; by then your bones will have rotted away, yet the canopy shall not yet be finished.
He asked his mother again, "Is there no hope for the canopy?"

Hearing that there is death and that the physical body must decay, and realizing that his past merits would soon come to an end, he was struck with trepidation and fear, reflecting that in this world of men, death is inevitable.
He replied to his mother, saying,
"I only pray that you will grant me leave to leave home and study the Way.
His mother was deeply grieved, yet she did not oppose his wish.
The mother said to him:
"I will permit you to leave the household life on the condition that, once you have accomplished the Way, you must return to see me;
only then shall I grant my consent."
He replied, "As you command;
when the Way is perfected, I shall return.

He immediately went to the forests and thickets, shaved off his beard and hair, donned the dharma robes, and practiced diligently in a quiet place. With unremitting vigor, he exhausted all defilements and attained the path of a pratyekabuddha.
While traveling through various kingdoms, districts, towns, and villages, he brought blessings and salvation to sentient beings, planting roots of goodness for them.
Suddenly remembering his mother’s longing, he ascended into the air like a king of geese and returned to the palace of his native land to meet with her.
From the highest to the lowest within the palace, all who witnessed the Daoist’s supernatural powers were filled with joy;
the king and his eighty-four thousand court ladies together entreated him to remain.
The Daoist was compassionate and benevolent, and as he did not oppose anyone, he accepted their invitation.
The ladies-in-waiting then constructed a hermitage in the rear garden of the palace for him to reside in. He took up lodging therein.
The entire palace provided him with offerings of food, clothing, bedding, and medicines as required, and performed rites of worship morning and evening.
Yet, throughout all the world, the strong grow old; the robust inevitably fall ill; and those who are born must all die.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha relinquished his life within the palace gardens. The entire court and the ladies-in-waiting offered him funeral rites with firewood, oil, flowers, and incense; they collected his bones and erected a stupa, where they paid homage morning and evening, burning incense and lighting lamps.
"At that time, King Mahādeva, having completed his circuit of the four quarters and returned, visited his rear garden. Seeing this stūpa there, he turned to his attendants and asked:
'For what reason is this here?'"
The court lady replied:
"This is the youngest son of the Holy King; having left his home to study the Way, he passed away here, and this stupa has been erected for him."
Thereupon, he asked again:
"Whose son are you?
For what reason have you left the home life?"
He then summoned his mother and asked her,
"Is this your son? She replied:
"Indeed," he replied.
He was asked again:
"For what reason do you train in the Path?"
His mother said to the king:
"In the past, when this child saw the King going out on a tour, he immediately asked me:
'I do not know when the King’s seven-jeweled parasol will revolve above my head?'"
The concubine then said:
"The Crown Prince should succeed and inherit the holy king; through a succession of a thousand sons, you, whose bones will rot and decay, shall forever have no hope."
When the son heard the concubine’s words, he was filled with sorrow and feared death; he sought to go forth and study the Way.
The concubine always granted him permission, and through diligent study, he perfected the Way.
We, the concubines, request to remain here and provide offerings for the rest of our lives, establishing this stūpa.
The King asked again:
"Is it because of this canopy that you have come to practice the Way?
He replied:

"So be it. Out of compassion for his son—who had practiced the Way throughout his life yet failed to obtain the *chhatra* (parasol) during his lifetime—the king now placed a parasol over the top of his stupa.
The king then made this vow:
"I now offer this canopy to the stupa of the Attained Way; by the karmic reward of this merit, may I attain the Buddha-way and deliver all sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
The king’s heart was struck with awe; he realized that the world is impermanent and that none can escape death. He therefore installed his crown prince to succeed him to the sacred throne.

The king renounced the four continents, the seven treasures, his thousand sons, and his eighty-four thousand palace ladies; he shaved off his beard and hair, became a śramaṇa, and practiced the Way in a quiet place. He cultivated the four pure abodes—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—for the remainder of his life, and upon his passing, was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"In your estimation, what do you think?
Is this Great King Deva anyone other than a person of distinction?"
Do not hold such a view; it was I myself who did so.
At that time, I offered a single parasol to a stupa of a Pratyekabuddha. By virtue of this meritorious retribution, I became a Wheel-Turning King upon this earth countless times;
furthermore, as a Heavenly King above, I enjoyed boundless blessings throughout the heavens and the world.
"With the remaining merit from that single parasol, I shall become a Wheel-Turning King over the four continents two thousand five hundred times in this world.
Ānanda asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"Why do you not accept this single parasol?
The Buddha said:

"This is the merit of my tenure as a Wheel-Turning King in one lifetime. The reason I have set it aside and do not accept it is that, through this karmic reward, I wish to provide for those who receive my Dharma transformation and become disciples—whether they be male or female practitioners—in the future degenerate age, so that they shall never lack food, clothing, bedding, or medicine for illness."
When the Dharma of the Buddhas of the past had completely vanished, those who were practicing the Way were unable to practice it due to either fear or the distress of hunger and poverty.

When the True Dharma has completely vanished and it is the final age, if there are those who leave home to study the Way within my Dharma-transformation, donning the dharma robes and professing the Buddha as their teacher, yet still keep wives and raise children—even such people will still receive offerings from others; how much more so for those who diligently cultivate and uphold the prohibitive precepts and maintain pure conduct? How could they not receive offerings until the very end of my Dharma?
The King of Rājagṛha issued an edict throughout his domain, ordering that a new bridge be constructed across the river so that the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones might cross it by means of it.
The kingdom of Vaiśālī likewise constructed a bridge, desiring to allow the Buddha to pass through.
The nāgas of the Ganges River interlaced their bodies to form a bridge, inviting the Buddha to cross it.
At that time, the Buddha reflected:
"If I were to cross by means of the bridge constructed for Rājagṛha, I fear that the kingdom of Vaiśālī and its nāga kings would harbor feelings of resentment."
"If I cross by means of the bridge constructed at Vaiśālī, I fear that Ajātaśatru and the nāga will harbor resentment.
If I wish to cross by means of the nāga-bridge, I fear that both kings will feel animosity.
The Buddha again reflected:
"Now I shall manifest my divided bodies so that Buddhas may pass over all three bridges.

As the Buddha approached the bridge, King Ajātaśatru, together with his retinue of several hundred million sentient beings, made offerings of incense, flowers, various jewels, and music to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of noble ones.

The king, together with his ministers and a great multitude numbering in the hundreds of millions, prostrated themselves on the ground, seeking refuge and repenting for their transgressions; they followed the Buddha weeping as he departed.

The Buddha manifested his supernatural transformations, appearing upon both the Bridge of the Two Kings and the Bridges of the Dragons, accompanied by the assembly of holy ones, while devas, nāgas, and spirits crossed the river upon the bridges.
The King of Rājagṛha, the King of Vaiśālī, and the various nāgas of the Ganges each saw the Buddha leading the great assembly across the river upon the bridge they themselves had built;
none of them knew or saw that there were other Buddhas on other bridges, each seeing only their own bridge as the Buddha ascended it to cross the river.
Just as the Buddha had finished crossing the river, he saw eighty-four thousand hungry ghosts with smoke and fire issuing from their bodies.
Among them, those who had not yet attained the Way were terrified by this fire, wondering, "What great conflagration is this?"
It was as if a great mountain were being consumed by fire; seeing this great conflagration, some approached the water while others remained far from it.
Ānanda, knowing the thoughts of all the people, knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Buddha, God among Gods!..."
The Buddha is most supreme and most venerable; he is the most honored in all the heavens above and the world below.
Among all sentient beings, there are none who do not feel terror upon seeing this fire.
What kind of fire is this?
"I pray that the Buddha will explain for the sake of all sentient beings what kind of fire this is.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"These hungry ghosts were in their previous lives those who did not encounter the Buddha, nor hear the Dharma, nor see the community of bhikṣus; they did not know that there is sin and merit in the world, and thus they were born as hungry ghosts."
Now, seeing the Buddha, they all rushed forward toward him, prostrating themselves with their heads to the ground, kneeling for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Buddha, God among Gods!

Most supreme and most venerable, the Buddha—out of compassion for all sentient beings, from those that fly and crawl to all forms of life within the heavens above and the earth below—is the father and mother of all sentient beings.
"I have fallen among the hungry ghosts; may the Buddha deliver me, and I shall likewise be as one among the class of all sentient beings.
The Buddha, knowing the seeds sown by the hungry ghost in previous lives, asked the hungry ghost for the sake of all sentient beings:
"What actions did you sow in your previous life that you are now a hungry ghost?"
The hungry ghost said:
"In my previous life, although I saw the Buddha, I did not know there was a Buddha;
although I saw the Dharma, I did not know there was a Dharma."
Although one sees the community of bhikṣus, one does not know that there is a community of bhikṣus.
I myself do not perform meritorious deeds, nor do I teach others to perform meritorious deeds; what kind of merit could there be in performing such deeds?
What kind of transgression is there in failing to perform meritorious deeds?
Seeing others perform merit, one constantly mocks them;
seeing others commit transgressions, one always feels joy in one's heart.
The Buddha asked the hungry ghost:
"Since you were born into this realm of hungry ghosts until now, how many hundreds of years have passed?
The hungry ghost replied:
“I have lived for seventy thousand years.
The Buddha asked the hungry ghost:
“Having lived for seventy thousand years, what kind of food and drink do you consume?”
"What food can we obtain?
The hungry ghosts replied, "In our past lives, we committed extremely evil deeds; when we encountered even a small amount of water, it would immediately vanish and become invisible."
When they reach great waters, they are pursued by ghosts, spirits, nāgas, and rākṣasas, who say:
"In your previous lives you sowed evil; why have you now come so close to these rivers and seas?"

"Even though he encounters great dragons raining down upon the whole world, thinking he has found rain to drench his body, he instead encounters pebbles and hot sand, or even falls upon burning charcoal."
The Buddha asked the hungry ghost,
"Throughout your life, for seventy thousand years, what have you eaten and drunk?
The hungry ghost replied to the Buddha:
"If there are parents, relatives, or kinsmen in the world who call out their names and perform meritorious deeds on their behalf, they will obtain a small amount of food;
those for whom no such merit is performed will not obtain food or drink."
The hungry ghosts joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have long been afflicted by hunger and thirst.
O Buddha, God among Gods, you who have compassion for all sentient beings, please now grant these hungry ghosts a small measure of food and drink."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Take this bowl, fetch some water, and offer it as alms to the hungry ghosts.
Ānanda then took the bowl, fetched water, and gave it to the hungry ghosts.
The hungry ghosts said to the Buddha,
"This single bowl of water will not satisfy even one person, let alone eighty-four thousand.
The Buddha spoke to the hungry ghosts:
"The eighty-four thousand [hungry ghosts] took this bowl-water and, with a sincere heart, offered it as alms to the Buddha and his disciples.
The eighty-four thousand hungry ghosts knelt for a long time and offered it, saying:
"Because we failed to practice giving in our previous lives, we have now been born among the hungry ghosts."

"Now that I have nothing else, I offer this bowl of water as a gift to the Buddha and his disciples, so that all hungry ghosts may, by virtue of this merit, distance themselves from the three evil realms and, in their future births, obtain teachers no different from the Buddha."

The hungry ghost passed the water to Ānanda; Ānanda took the water and gave it to the Buddha to taste a single mouthful, then passed it to each of his twelve hundred and fifty disciples for them to taste a single mouthful.
The Buddha said to the hungry ghosts,
"Enter the great river to drink its water and also to bathe. However,
the dragons, ghosts, and spirits of the rivers and seas obstructed them, so that they were unable to bathe or drink.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King Sāgara and the various spirits and deities:
"Why do you cherish this boundless water?
The dragons, spirits, and deities replied:
"I do not begrudge this water, for it is defiled by hungry ghosts.
The Buddha said to the Dragon King Sāgara and the spirits:
"From countless kalpas past, your own bodies have also been such as these."
"Because you cherished the waters of the boundless ocean, you shall later take this same body; yet, due to your stinginess and greed, you will be reborn as a hungry ghost.
When the dragon kings of the various seas and the spirits heard the Buddha’s words, they all returned to the sea, allowing all the hungry ghosts to drink their fill and bathe.
He emerged once more, circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated before him, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Buddha, God among Gods!
You know the future and the past; when shall I be liberated from this body of a hungry ghost?"
The Buddha said:

“Because of this single bowl of water, when Maitreya Buddha appears in the world in the future, at a time when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, all those who were hungry ghosts shall obtain human bodies and all attain the path of Arhatship;
furthermore, all those in the assembly who hear of the merit of this act of giving shall attain the resolve for the correct and true path.”
All the hungry ghosts circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves, and departed.

Countless kings, ministers, elders, householders, and citizens of the kingdom of Vaiśālī prostrated with their five limbs touching the ground, casting themselves at the Buddha’s feet; they took refuge in the Triple Gem and welcomed the World-Honored One with incense, flowers, music, silken canopies, banners, and streamers. Flowers covered the ground everywhere as they made offerings along the road, continuing day after day without ceasing.

Upon reaching the city, the Buddha, together with the assembly of noble ones, devas, nāgas, and spirits, went to the city gate. With his golden arm and hand marked by the auspicious signs, he touched the threshold of the gate and, in the eightfold pure Brahma-voice, spoke this verse:
"Whatever classes of sentient beings exist within the realm of earth—those who walk or dwell upon the ground, as well as those in the midst of space."
"Show loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, Causing each to find peace and rest;
Day and night, with diligent and focused application, Practice and uphold all wholesome dharmas.
Having spoken this verse, the earth immediately shook in six ways. The Buddha then entered the city.
The spirits and deities dwelling in the air ascended into the sky and dispersed;

the spirits and deities who travel upon the earth vied with one another to rush out through the gates, but the city gates could not contain them, and they all broke through in their headlong flight until the walls collapsed as they emerged.
At that time, all impurities, latrines, filth, and foul odors within the city sank deep into the earth; high and low ground became level with one another, and the ditches and pits were all made even.
The blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, and the lame walked; the insane regained their composure and the sick were healed.

Elephants, horses, oxen, and other livestock lowed and neighed in harmony; *konghou* lutes and other musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, their tones blending in perfect accord.

The pearl bracelets on the women’s arms produced harmonious and wondrous sounds; the vessels, jars, and flasks naturally emitted voices that were soft, pleasant, and resonant with the sound of the sublime Dharma.
Treasures hidden within the earth spontaneously emerge.
Just as all sentient beings who encounter heat and thirst find relief upon obtaining cool water— drinking it, bathing in it, and attaining peace and rest—
so too are all the various diseases of the entire city cured and they attain liberation.

The Buddha, together with the great assembly, then returned out of the city. Pervaded by great compassion and mercy, he desired to bestow great protection upon sentient beings; he circumambulated the city on all sides, offering incantations and prayers at every gate, expounding the wondrous Dharma to eliminate calamities and bring forth auspiciousness. Thus, the illnesses and pestilences throughout the entire kingdom were entirely eradicated, and the realm became peaceful in its entirety.
Thereupon, Caìmíng stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“As previously promised, you have shown compassion; I only pray that tomorrow, for the sake of all sentient beings, you will turn your light toward us and deign to visit our humble home for a meal of simple vegetables.”
The Buddha silently gave his consent.
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, they circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated before him, and withdrew.
Returning home, they prepared a meal of a hundred flavors, pure, fragrant, and clean, with brilliant colors and sweet taste.
He adorned his home, hanging silken banners and canopies, arranging couches and cushions, sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground, scattering flowers, and burning incense.
Having prepared all the offerings, he knelt for a long time from within the gate, burning incense and addressing the Buddha from afar:
"I pray that you will deign to manifest your divine spirit here."
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded his disciples to don their robes and take up their alms bowls, proceeding to the home of the elder Cāru to accept his invitation.

Upon arriving at the gate, Cāru, with solemn reverence, offered flowers, incense, and music, inviting the Buddha to enter the house. The Buddha and the assembly of noble ones took their respective seats in order.
At that time, Caìmíng took up a golden pitcher and personally went to provide water for washing. With his own hands, he measured out the portions with impartiality for those of high and low station.
When the meal was finished, he again provided water for washing, knelt down on his right knee with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will extend his fourfold impartial mind and accept another three days of my invitation as it is now."
The Buddha remained silent, thereby granting his consent.
Thereupon, Caiming provided for the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones with various kinds of fragrant and pure offerings, just as on the first day.

When the four days had concluded, he offered a golden cloth worth one hundred thousand [coins] to the *sthavira* (elder), followed by cloths worth ninety thousand in descending order, down to a cloth worth ten thousand coins for the lowest-ranking seat, serving as the *dakṣiṇā* (offering).
His wife immediately rose, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Heaven among Heavens! You bestow your compassion upon all beings;
I pray that you will deign to let your divine light remain and accept this humble servant’s request to stay for four more days."
The Buddha granted his silent consent.
His wife made offerings for the first day, the second day, and so on until the fourth day; the food and drink were fragrant and pure, remaining identical in quality throughout.
When the four days had concluded, he again offered to the World-Honored One ten thousand gold pieces worth of fine cloth, followed by nine thousand pieces, and finally ten thousand coins.
Then, the son Cai Ming rose and approached the Buddha; kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O, Heaven among Heavens!..."
"Since my parents have already accepted four days' worth of meals each, I pray that you will deign to show me compassion and pity, and accept my invitation for four days.
The Buddha likewise gave his silent assent.

For four days, the son served with reverence and diligence; the food and drink were as delicious as those provided by his parents. He then offered a stack of gold cloth worth one hundred thousand coins to the World-Honored One, followed by ninety thousand, and finally ten thousand coins.
The daughter-in-law rose again, knelt with her head to the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One of vast compassion!
Having already accepted the offerings from my mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband, I would be fortunate if you would, as before, accept these for four more days."
The Buddha again accepted in silence.

The food and delicacies provided were no different from before; it continued for four days, and on each occasion, he was given a hundred thousand gold pieces for the upper seat, ninety thousand for the next seat, and ten thousand coins for the lower seat as his *dakṣiṇā*.

The members of the household, both great and small, sat before the Buddha and received his instructions. The Buddha proclaimed and expounded for them the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—the Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones, whereby they severed the twenty-two fetters of the weary mind and realized the stream-entry of the Truths.
The kings, ministers, elders, householders, and all the people of the kingdom of Vaiśālī all conceived this thought:
"Has the Buddha come to our country solely for the sake of one man of talent and wisdom?"
Their minds were all filled with resentment.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantrymen all gathered together and headed toward Caiming’s house, intending to destroy his residence so that they might see the World-Honored One.
The great assembly trembled, and a resounding noise arose; the Buddha, having foreseen it all in advance, asked Ānanda:
"What sound is this outside?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
The King of Vaiśālī, his ministers, elders, and all the people, both high and low, harbored feelings of resentment:

"When the World-Honored One entered our country, we invited him with our talents and wisdom to return to our home; yet he remained stubbornly at home alone until the sixteenth day, so that none of us were able to see him."
"Because they were dissatisfied with this, they have gathered here, desiring to see the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go out and comfort these people; let them harbor no feelings of resentment. Those who wish to see the Buddha, allow them to enter."
Ānanda delivered the command to the great assembly, saying:
"Please grant permission for him to enter.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s instruction, the anger of the king, the ministers, and all the people vanished instantly; not even a trace of resentment remained, just as rain settles rising dust.
He then entered to see the Buddha, prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs touching it, and bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet.
The great assembly was so vast that the house could not contain them;

those remaining outside were numerous. Out of universal compassion, the Buddha transformed Caiming’s house into lapis lazuli, making it transparent both inside and out so that everyone could see one another clearly.

Thereupon, Caiming prepared seats and couches, woolen rugs and fine carpets, as well as various utensils for food; he provided vessels made of crystal, lapis lazuli, gold, silver, and diverse precious gems.
When the great assembly had finished eating, Cai Ming then stepped forward and addressed the World-Honored One and the various honored guests:

"We live in frugality and subsist on simple vegetarian fare; yet you have condescended to grace us with your presence. We pray that you will accept our humble offering of these food vessels and bedding seats."
At that time, the great assembly was struck with astonishment; they all sighed in admiration, saying:
"The Elder’s brilliance and wisdom have established his reputation not falsely; it truly accords with his virtue."
He established great acts of almsgiving and presented precious vessels as offerings, reaching everywhere without exception.
How could the wealth and treasures within his household possibly be calculated, let alone those belonging to the fourfold assembly of disciples and the great multitude?
Their minds were filled with doubt, wondering:

"What merit does this wise and brilliant elder possess that he has invited the Buddha and the great assembly for the sixteenth day? He has provided offerings and gifts to the king, ministers, and commoners throughout the entire kingdom, so that all may partake of the nectar of immortality."
"Is this the result of merit from a previous life,
or virtue from this present life?
Ānanda, immediately perceiving the doubts in the minds of the assembly, knelt with palms joined and stepped forward to address the Buddha:
“The great assembly wonders at which field of merit the Elder Cai Ming has extensively planted the roots of virtue;

under what enlightened teacher did he receive instruction that he has now attained this karmic retribution of boundless wealth, his mind clear and conduct pure, having first tasted the nectar of immortality?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will now reveal his past practices to resolve all doubts!
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the entire great assembly:
"Listen with single-minded attention!
I shall now resolve the doubts in your mind.
In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī.
Not far from the city was a mountain named Ṛṣipatana; within that mountain were ponds, forests, trees, flowers, and fruits, whose bliss was beyond compare.
When there is a Buddha in the world, he dwells therein together with his disciples;
if there is no Buddha in the world, pratyekabuddhas reside there;
and if there are no pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhist practitioners and immortals then dwell there; thus, it is never left desolate.
For this reason, it is named "Abode of the Immortals.

At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha dwelling in the mountain. Rising early, he washed his face and rinsed his mouth; donning his dharma robes and carrying his alms bowl, he left the mountain to seek food. Before he had reached a village, he encountered a violent storm.
Not far from the road, there was an official fruit orchard with a park supervisor in charge.
Seeing smoke rising from it, the Daoist went to him and said, "I encountered wind and rain on my journey;
I would be grateful if you would allow me to enter your quarters to warm myself by the fire and dry my clothes."
He immediately invited him in, gathered firewood, and lit a fire to dry his clothes.
Once the clothes were dry and his body warmed, the wind and rain subsided slightly; he put on his garments and wished to depart.
The garden supervisor asked,
"Venerable holy man!
Where do you wish to go?"
He replied: "Worthy one!
All those with form take clothing and food as their life."
I have left home to study and subsist by begging for food;
if I do not obtain food, my life and spirit will not be sustained, my faculties will not be settled, and I will be unable to contemplate the Way.
The park keeper replied, “This is the simple fare of a poor household;
its color is coarse and its flavor is sour. If you would deign to accept it with a sweetened heart, I pray you stay and do not depart.
The Pratyekabuddha answered:
"I study the Way and seek food not for the sake of its color or flavor, but merely to sustain my body.
If you permit me to eat, I shall stay here and not go.
Thereupon, the garden supervisor returned home to fetch rice.
Upon arriving home, he asked his wife,
"Is the meal prepared?
She replied:
"It is finished.
According to the custom of that country regarding meals, rice was divided and eaten separately.
The husband said to his wife:
"Bring me my portion; I have an important guest whom I wish to feed.
His wife then thought to herself:
"My husband is a man and ought to perform manual labor, braving both cold and heat; if he does not eat, he will be unable to perform such labor."
"I am but a woman; staying at home in leisure, I may take my own portion to serve this guest.
Her son spoke again:
"Our parents are advanced in years; you may eat from your own portion and give mine to him."
Her daughter-in-law said:
"Since my mother-in-law and husband have promised to entertain guests, and I am young and strong enough to endure hunger and thirst, I beg that my portion be used for entertaining the guests."
The Great Man then said:
"Each of you has a virtuous mind wishing to give; you may together set aside a portion from your shares, which will be sufficient to feed the guests."
Thereupon, each of them reduced their own portion of rice.
The garden supervisor thought again:
"The Daoists' robes are torn and worn, exposing their bodies."
He then asked his wife,
"Do you have even a little clothing at home?
His wife replied:
"In my home there is only a single set of layered robes; when receiving guests or opening the door, we must share this garment between us, for we possess nothing else.
The husband replied to his wife:
"Because we failed to practice charity in our previous lives, we now endure poverty and low status, unable to keep pace with others."
If one does not practice giving now, when will this state of poverty and lowliness ever come to an end?
Those who possess wealth, nobility, and honor, and for whom food and clothing appear spontaneously, all owe this to the merit of their benevolent giving in previous lives.
"I shall continue my charitable giving without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Furthermore, I have no need for guests to attend, nor for doorkeepers to answer, nor for changing my attire.
Taking the cotton cloth and the food, the entire family went together to the place where the practitioner was; there they washed their hands and offered the meal.

When the practitioners had finished eating, they rinsed their mouths and washed their bowls. The four men then respectfully folded the bedding and offered it to the Pratyekabuddha, who immediately put it on.

Without using verbal teachings to convert others, the Pratyekabuddha manifested supernatural powers to delight and awaken sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the path. He addressed the host, saying:
"Because you were able to bestow this gift and provide offerings to the practitioners, your resolve has been strengthened; you should now give rise to a great vow."
Having finished speaking, he ascended into the air, where he sat cross-legged, stood, and performed walking meditation, manifesting as pratyekabuddhas that filled the void.
Each manifested transformations, emitting water and fire from their bodies; the water did not extinguish the fire, nor did the fire invade the water, displaying various such miraculous changes.
Flying through the air, he returned to Mount Xianju.
The garden superintendent and his attendants were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they joined their palms in reverence, bowed their heads in supplication, and made this vow:

"By virtue of the merit gained from bestowing [this gift] today upon the sagely, wise, and divine Daoist, may we be freed from the three evil realms—the destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals."

Wherever they are born, they always gather together; in both the heavens and the human world, they enjoy abundance, peace, and security. With the power of awakened wisdom and the Way, they partake of the flavor of ambrosia like a holy and enlightened teacher;
if they encounter such an enlightened teacher, their spiritual virtue becomes exceptionally sublime.
The Buddha told the great assembly:
"The park keeper at that time was Cai Ming;
his wife, son, and daughter-in-law were all these very people."

At that time, they made offerings with one heart to the Honored Pratyekabuddha; from then until now, for ninety-one kalpas, they have not again fallen into the three miserable realms, but have received the retribution of vast blessings. Whether in the heavens or the human world, their families have gathered together, never parting from one another.

At that time, he made this vow: "May I partake of the nectar of immortality, awaken to the Way and attain liberation, and encounter a most excellent teacher. Because of these conditions, he has now encountered me and met with supreme enlightenment—boundless and beyond compare—and now partakes of the nectar of immortality, just as his former teachers did.

At that time, the great assembly, having heard the Buddha proclaim the retribution of meritorious deeds, was without exception filled with joy; their hearts were delighted and their minds purified as they took refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. Their karmic obstructions and fetters were dissolved, and some received the five precepts while others left the household life to study the Way.

Thereupon, within the assembly, four thousand people all attained the fruits of the stage of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; incalculable numbers of people resolved upon the Mahāyāna, their minds becoming irreversible.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose and departed from the house, and the entire great assembly prostrated themselves and withdrew.

The Buddha and the great assembly traveled to the Nanda Grove tree-vihāra; when Nanda heard that the Buddha had arrived at her grove with the great assembly of sages, her heart was filled with immeasurable joy. She immediately prepared her carriage and, accompanied by her attendants, went to the grove to see the Buddha.

Upon arrival, she descended from her precious chariot like lightning flashing from a cloud; she entered the garden with a graceful gait, her attire and countenance surpassing those of the celestial maidens of the Heaven of Auspiciousness (Kṛtavarman).
The devas dwelling in the garden trees all turned their eyes toward him.

Seeing this, the Buddha knew that these were the Māra’s emissaries who had come to destroy his pure precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. He then addressed the śramaṇas with a Brahma-voice:

"The daughter of the Nyagrodha tree has arrived; each of you must restrain your minds. Each must grasp the sword and bow of diligence, prepare for yourselves the arrows of wisdom, don the armor of meditative concentration, and mount the chariot of the prohibitive precepts to wage war against the afflictions."

"You should reflect upon all that women possess: they are deceptive like gold-plated coins; their skin is as thin as a fly's wing, covering foul impurities; they are a collection of flesh and blood held together by sinews and bones; with rheum from the eyes, mucus, saliva, sweat, and grime upon the body—if these are not washed away.
Reflecting in this way, observe the female body to restrain the deluded mind of lustful desire."

Observe closely this skeletal dwelling: bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with clothing, and adorned with flowers and silks. It is just as if a painter were to stand before a wall, applying a base of clay and mud to cover impurities, and then painting it with various colors. The body of a woman is exactly like this; one should contemplate and understand this clearly, thereby extinguishing lustful thoughts.
Those who wish to study the Way must first harmonize their minds; only then can they attain peace. If one does not first harmonize the mind, it will be too late for regrets later.

Erroneous conduct leads to delusion and wandering, like a horse tethered to a hitching post; as its life draws to a close, its wishes and intentions conflict, and it ultimately fails to achieve liberation.
If there are those who perceive forms and their minds follow delusion— reckoning the impermanent as permanent, perceiving pleasure in suffering, reckoning the non-self as self,

and perceiving the impure as pure— if they awaken with wisdom to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity, and realize these truths, they will immediately leave behind the long journey of the afflictions and hardships of birth and death.
The Buddha taught this instruction to his disciples, who all received and upheld it, practicing it with single-minded devotion.

When the maiden Āmrapālī saw the Buddha, he was like the sun emerging from the clouds, radiant with golden light; her mind became pure and serene, and she prostrated herself on the ground, bowing her head at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha told the daughter of Amrapālī:
"Women’s minds are prone to indulgence and are deluded by attachment to the five desires.
That you have been able to restrain and turn back your mind, coming to where the Buddha is to delight in the transformation of the wondrous Dharma—this is your greatest benefit."
It is not considered extraordinary that a man is stable and grave, has thin defilements and impurities, and delights in receiving the transformation of the Dharma;
for a woman is entangled in the net of worldly afflictions, circling and obstructed within them, unaware of the essential way of escape.

All the worlds are suffering, empty, and impermanent; they cannot be relied upon or trusted. Vigor swiftly invades the prime of youth; old age robs one of their complexion; death seizes the span of life; and peril assails what is secure.
To escape this affliction, one must single-mindedly receive the Dharma and diligently practice its observance; only then can one be freed from this suffering.
Women harbor resentment and hatred, yet when they encounter others, their behavior is exceedingly foul; they are also intensely attached to the parting from those they love and cherish.
As women, they are never far removed from these two matters.

Therefore, women should diligently serve the Dharma; they may thus avoid encounters with enmity and partings from those they love, no longer encounter birth, old age, sickness, and death, and bring all suffering to total cessation.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s various wondrous teachings on the impurity of women, the daughter of Nala felt deep shame and remorse. She immediately rose, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms, and addressed the Buddha:
“I pray that you will deign to show me compassion, and together with the assembly of noble ones, come to my home to receive a meal.”
The Buddha silently accepted.

Thereupon, the daughter of the Naga bowed her head and withdrew; she returned home and prepared a meal of a hundred flavors, sweet, crisp, and exquisite. She set out banners, canopies, seats, and cushions, sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, burned incense, and scattered flowers. Kneeling for a long time, she invited the Buddha, saying: "The hour has arrived;
we pray that you and the assembly of noble ones will deign to turn back and grace us with your presence."
The Buddha and his disciples donned their robes, took up their alms bowls, and went to the home of the girl Āmrapālī.
With flowers, incense, and musical performances, she invited the Buddha into her house; they each took their seats, whereupon she personally served them with water and presented them with food.

When the meal was finished and they had rinsed their mouths, the Buddha extensively expounded upon the meritorious rewards of giving and the fruits of moral restraint; he taught that the pleasures of gods and humans cannot endure long, being fraught with peril, destruction, and separation, and thus cannot be relied upon. He further taught that only the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path of the Sages lead to great peace and eternal freedom from sorrow and affliction.
Their hearts were filled with joy; their doubts were dispelled and their fetters untied, and they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The assembly sat there wondering:
"What merit did the maiden Āmrapālī possess in her previous life that she was born from a flower on a tree, so exceptionally beautiful and fair?"
The worthy Ānanda, perceiving that the assembly harbored doubts, knelt with palms joined and stepped forward to address the Buddha:

"The entire assembly sits here in doubt: in what field of merit did the daughter of King Naya plant the roots of virtue in her previous life, that she has now encountered the World-Honored One and partaken of the medicine of ambrosia?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In a past age, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, that Buddha completed his buddha-work and then relinquished his life-span."
At that time, there was a king named Śubhagrīva who made offerings to the śarīra, erecting a stūpa of the seven precious jewels one yojana in height.
All sentient beings offered lamps, burned incense, and presented flowers, canopies, and silken banners as acts of worship and service.
At that time, there were many women who wished to make offerings to the stūpa; they joined together to sweep the ground around it.
Then, a dog’s excrement defiled the stūpa grounds, and one woman took it up in her hand and discarded it.
Furthermore, there was another woman who saw him clearing dog dung from the ground with his hand;
she spat upon him, laughed at him, and said, "Your hands are defiled; you must not come near me again."
The woman rebuked him in return:
"You wretched lecher! My hands would have been purified simply by washing them with water.
The Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, is worthy of boundless reverence."
Having cleared away the impurities with his hands, he then washed his hands and circumambulated the stupa while making this aspiration:
"Just as the filth of this stupa ground has now been removed by my sweeping, may the toil and defilements of my future lives be extinguished, and may I be pure and free from all impurity."
"The women who were sweeping the ground of the stupa at that time are the women present in this assembly today.

Those who swept the ground then, aspiring to extinguish the dust of afflictions and partake of the flavor of the nectar of immortality—among them, the woman who used her hand to remove the dog dung is the woman from the city of Pāṭaliputra."

At that time, he made a vow not to encounter filth, so that wherever he was born, it would be pure; by virtue of this meritorious retribution, he was never born from the foul and impure place of a womb, but was always born from a flower.
"Because at that time you uttered a single evil sound, reviling me as a 'prostitute,' you now receive this name of 'prostitute.

" The Buddha then explained in detail the retribution for good and evil: the honor, joy, and pleasures of the heavens and the world, and the suffering of the three evil realms, where beings devour one another and wail in bitter grief.

At that time, the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had taught, took refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; they purified their body, speech, and mind, and practiced the ten wholesome paths of action;
and countless people each established the aspiration for the Way within the three vehicles.
All were filled with joy; they circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves, and departed.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One returned to the vihāra.
This concludes the *Buddha-bhāṣita-dhūtakarṣaṇa-sūtra*.
